performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
question: How can a drinking song keep returning to the same line of despair and still sound defiant?
intro: A host is told to hold back the wine until the singer has sung a song of sorrow. The refrain, “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”, comes three times, each a semitone higher, and an ape howls on the graves before the cups are drained. This is the first song of one live 1939 Amsterdam performance of the whole cycle.

sections.label: A · Allegro pesante — the song of sorrow
B · Wenn der Kummer naht — the garden laid waste
R · First refrain — Dunkel ist das Leben
C · Tempo I subito — host, lute and wine
R′ · Second refrain, a semitone higher
sections.mNote: same words a semitone higher, in A♭

sections.label: A′ · Seht dort hinab — the ape on the graves
sections.mNote: flutter-tongued opening music returns, with the tenor

sections.label: R″ · Jetzt nehmt den Wein — third refrain
sections.mNote: third refrain, higher still, after the cup is emptied

cues.title: A fortissimo opening
cues.text: The song begins at once, loud: a horn call, trilling flutes and clarinets, and trumpets with mutes and rapid tongued notes. The heading is Allegro pesante, with the note “whole bars, not fast”. There is no slow introduction.
cues.evidence: The first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; IMSLP #20582, printed p. 3) gives the heading, the horn and trumpet writing (mit Dämpfer, Zungenstoß) and the flutter-tongued woodwinds. The recording is silent at 0:00 (−48 dB) and at −11.4 dB by 0:05.

cues.title: A tenor against the full orchestra
cues.text: The tenor enters “mit voller Kraft” — with full strength — singing “Schon winkt der Wein im goldnen Pokale”. The wine already beckons in the golden cup, but do not drink yet. His part sits high against the full orchestra; Adorno said the tenor should suggest a “denatured voice” in the Chinese (falsetto) style.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 5) marks the tenor’s entry Mit voller Kraft; the Mahler Foundation page for this song (https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-lied-1-das-trinklied-vom-jammer-der-erde/) describes the tenor’s struggle at the top of his range and Adorno’s remark. A boundary at 0:12 (0.80) is consistent with the entry, but the entry time is not claimed.

cues.title: Li Bai’s song of sorrow
cues.text: The source is Li Bai’s “Song of Sorrow” (Beige xing), whose cry “bei lai hu” means “how sorrowful”. Neither the Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s French nor Hans Heilmann’s German has a refrain. Bethge supplies “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”, four times; Mahler keeps three.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Das Trinklied page (http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Das_Trinklied.htm); Edwin K. C. Li, JRMA 150/2 (2025), Table 2 and the footnote on the refrain, which was not in Hervey de Saint-Denys or Heilmann and appeared four times in Bethge; the Mahler Foundation page for this song notes the omitted fourth refrain.

cues.title: Wenn der Kummer naht
cues.text: Around 0:58 (about bar 53 by proportion) the loud drinking music gives way to a hush: “Wenn der Kummer naht” — when sorrow comes near — marked düster, zart (gloomy, tender), at the same tempo. A solo violin and harps follow as “liegen wüst die Gärten der Seele”: the gardens of the soul lie waste.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 0:58 (0.69); onset density falls from 3.4 per second at 0:55 to 1.2 at 1:00 and 0.4 at 1:05, with the local key estimate B♭ major at 1:00–1:05 (0.70–0.72; not a chord identification). Utz Table 2 puts Sempre l’istesso tempo at m. 53 and 52 bars before it at Schuricht’s mean Tempo I of 52.8 a minute is about a minute, consistent with 0:58. The score (printed pp. 9–10, rehearsal figures 7–8) has Sempre l’istesso tempo, düster, zart, the text and a solo violin marked schmeichelnd.

cues.title: Three blows of 1907
cues.text: In 1907 Mahler resigned from the Vienna Court Opera (“because I can no longer endure the rabble”), signed a contract for New York’s Metropolitan Opera on 21 June, and lost his elder daughter Maria to scarlet fever and diphtheria within weeks. A doctor then found his heart defect.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538 (resignation, the contract of 21 June 1907, Maria’s death at Maiernigg, the valvular defect); the Mahler Foundation introduction lists the same three disasters.

cues.title: The first refrain: sehr ruhig
cues.text: Around 1:42 the tenor reaches the first “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”: very calm (sehr ruhig), very sustained (sehr getragen), over a solo horn and harp arpeggios, in G minor. It is the first of three statements, each a semitone higher than the last.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 1:42 (0.88) with G minor estimated at 1:45–2:05 (correlation 0.69–0.75) and low onset density (0.6–1.8 per second at 1:35–2:00). The score (printed pp. 11–12, rehearsal figures 10–11) has Zurückhaltend. Ruhig., Sehr ruhig, a horn marked Solo, harp arpeggios and the refrain text; Utz’s analysis (https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37) places the first refrain in G minor; the Mahler Foundation page says the refrain rises a semitone at each return.

cues.title: Tempo I subito: the loudest stretch
cues.text: The first speed returns at once, loud, with flutter-tongued flutes and clarinets, horns and open trumpets over rushing strings. The windows from 2:10 to 2:20 are among the five loudest of the whole song, and 2:20 is the single loudest. Listen for how suddenly the refrain’s hush is forgotten.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −11.9 dB at 2:00 to −5.1 dB at 2:05 and −3.6, −3.4 and −2.9 dB at 2:10, 2:15 and 2:20; the five loudest windows are 2:20, 7:40, 2:15, 2:10 and 7:35. The score (printed p. 13) marks Tempo I subito at rehearsal figure 12 with Flatterzunge in the winds and open trumpets.

cues.title: The host’s cellar
cues.text: Around 2:30 the tenor addresses the host: “Herr dieses Hauses! Dein Keller birgt die Fülle des goldenen Weins!” Lord of this house, your cellar holds golden wine in plenty. Soon after comes “Hier, diese Laute nenn’ ich mein!” — this lute I call mine.
cues.evidence: Key estimates read A major at 2:30–2:40 (0.44–0.67) and A minor at 2:45–2:50 (0.66–0.71) after the loud ritornello of 2:10–2:25. The score (printed pp. 15–17) gives these lines after the ritornello; their exact times are not claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harps and the lute
cues.text: In the stanza about lute and glasses (“Die Laute schlagen und die Gläser leeren, das sind die Dinge, die zusammenpassen”) two harps play soft patterns while the flutes and clarinets are marked p dolce. Listen for the thinner, sweeter sound after the cellar’s loud fanfares.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 18, rehearsal figure 18) marks harp figures p and dolce for the flutes and clarinets under this text. The recording is at a lower level around 2:55 (−11 dB, 0.8 onsets per second); the exact entrance is not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Ein voller Becher Weins”
cues.text: A full cup of wine at the right time, the tenor says, is worth more than all the kingdoms of this earth. The tenor’s line is marked glühend — glowing — in a flat-heavy key signature, and the audio reads an E♭-minor region around 3:10–3:25.
cues.evidence: Local key estimates read E♭ minor with correlation 0.73–0.76 at 3:10–3:20, level −13 to −16 dB at 3:15–3:20. The score (printed pp. 19–21) has the text, glühend, and a flat-heavy signature; Utz Table 2 gives the harmony of this stanza as E♭ minor / A♭.

cues.title: The refrain again, higher
cues.text: After “Reiche dieser Erde” the pace slackens (Rit., a tempo, sehr ruhig) and the second “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod!” arrives a semitone higher than the first, in A♭. Schuricht takes the refrains at about 36, 35 and 35 bars a minute against 53 for Tempo I, so each refrain is a near-halt.
cues.evidence: Level is −7.4 dB at 3:35, then −11.6 dB at 3:40 and −16.5 dB at 3:45, with onset density 0.2 per second at 3:45 and 0.0 at 3:50 and A♭ minor estimated at 3:55–4:10 (0.73–0.79). The score (printed pp. 21–22) has Rit., a tempo, sehr ruhig, and the refrain text. Tempo figures: Christian Utz, Musicologica Austriaca (2018), Table 4, https://musau.org/assets/Uploads/2018/Utz/Utz-Mahler-Table04.pdf (Schuricht 1939: refrains 36.4, 35.2, 34.6; Tempo I 52.8).

cues.title: The voice leaves; the orchestra plays on
cues.text: After the held “Tod!” the tenor is silent for over a minute. Around 4:10–4:35 the orchestra alone moves from the refrain’s hush towards a loud A♭ passage; harps, flutter-tongued flutes and marcato trumpet figures lead to strings marked sempre ff before the tenor’s return.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 3:54 (0.80), 4:12 (0.65), 4:28 (0.55), 4:36 (0.89) and 4:54 (0.68) with A♭ major estimated at 4:15–5:10 (0.62–0.91) and level −9.4 dB at 4:55 and 5:00. The score (printed pp. 23–26, rehearsal figures 25–30; Utz Table 2 gives an orchestral interlude of mm. 203–260) has Rit., a tempo, flutter-tonguing and sempre ff strings; the tenor is absent.

cues.title: Cylinders of Chinese music
cues.text: According to the Mahler Foundation’s chronology, in August 1908 Paul Hammerschlag visited Mahler at Toblach, heard him express interest in China and Chinese music, and bought him phonograph cylinders of Chinese music. What Mahler heard on them is not documented here.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, History: Das Lied von der Erde (https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/), 1908 entry for August; the chronology’s other entries were checked against Hefling’s Universal Edition introduction, which does not mention the cylinders.

cues.title: Das Firmament blaut ewig
cues.text: Around 5:00 loud strings in A♭ major, marked sempre ff, give way to the tenor: “Das Firmament blaut ewig und die Erde wird lange fest steh’n und aufblüh’n im Lenz.” The heavens stay blue and the earth will bloom again in spring. Man, the next lines say, will not.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is A♭ major with correlation up to 0.91 at 4:55, with level −9.4 dB at 4:55–5:00 and a fall to −15.4 dB at 5:05. The score (printed p. 26, rehearsal figures 30–31) has strings sempre ff and the tenor’s “Das Firmament”, marked p ma appassionato.

cues.title: An orchestral subordinate theme
cues.text: About 5:25 the level rises again over a ten-bar orchestral theme in F minor, the development’s subordinate theme, with the tenor silent. The mood darkens after the A♭-major radiance of “Das Firmament”, and the line is passed between woodwinds and strings.
cues.evidence: Level rises to −7.5, −6.6 and −5.6 dB at 5:25–5:35 with F minor and C minor estimated (0.76–0.85) at 5:30–5:40. Utz Table 2 (https://musau.org/assets/Uploads/2018/Utz/Utz-Mahler-Table02.pdf) places an instrumental subordinate theme in F at mm. 281–290; bar times are proportioned, not measured.

cues.title: “Du aber, Mensch”
cues.text: Around 5:45 the tenor turns on his listener: “Du aber, Mensch, wie lang lebst denn du?” — and you, man, how long do you live? It is marked leidenschaftlich, passionate, and begins a long intensification: harps and trilling woodwinds surround the question.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 29, rehearsal figure 35) has the text, leidenschaftlich, harps and woodwind trills; Utz places Leidenschaftlich at m. 291, 35 bars before the loud tutti that opens the ape scene at about 6:20, which puts it near 5:45. The time is a bar proportion, not a measurement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Not a hundred years
cues.text: “Nicht hundert Jahre darfst du dich ergötzen an all dem morschen Tande dieser Erde!” Not a hundred years may you delight in all the rotten baubles of this earth. Listen for the strings and winds sinking until, around 6:10, the song reaches one of its quietest windows outside its first and last seconds.
cues.evidence: The quietest 5-second windows include 6:10 and 6:15 (−24.6 and −22.6 dB; 0:00, 8:50 and 8:55 are also among the quietest), after F-minor and A♭-major estimates at 5:55–6:05. The score (printed pp. 30–31) has the text, then a diminuendo after “Erde!”.

cues.title: A ff tutti, then “Seht dort hinab!”
cues.text: Around 6:20 the level jumps by about thirteen decibels into a fortissimo tutti with glockenspiel, triangle, muted brass and trills. Within seconds the tenor cries “Seht dort hinab!” — look down there. The song’s strongest structural boundary falls here.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −22.6 dB at 6:15 to −9.4 dB at 6:20 and the strongest boundary of the song is at 6:22 (1.00); the level is −9.5 dB at 6:25 and −7.1 dB at 6:30. The score (printed pp. 31–32, rehearsal figures 39–40) has the ff tutti with glockenspiel, triangle and muted brass and then “Seht dort hinab!”; the tenor’s word is not timed.

cues.title: Moonlight on the graves
cues.text: “Im Mondschein auf den Gräbern hockt eine wild-gespenstische Gestalt” — in the moonlight on the graves squats a wildly ghostly shape. The level pulls back and the key leans towards E♭ minor; stopped horns and trombones sustain, and violas and cellos play snapped notes.
cues.evidence: Level falls to −12.7 dB at 6:35 with the key estimate E♭ minor (0.49–0.54) and onset density 0.4 per second at 6:35; the score (printed pp. 32–33, rehearsal figures 40–42) has the text, gestopft horns and gerissen strings.

cues.title: “Ein Aff’ ist’s!”
cues.text: “Ein Aff’ ist’s! Hört ihr, wie sein Heulen hinausgellt in den süßen Duft des Lebens!” An ape it is; hear how its howl shrieks out into the sweet scent of life. Trumpets, glockenspiel and triangle sound over restless strings as the loudness builds.
cues.evidence: Level is −7.3 to −5.5 dB at 6:40–6:55 and −5.7 to −5.8 dB at 7:00–7:10 with onset density up to 4.4 per second at 6:45. The score (printed p. 34, rehearsal figure 43) has the text, muted trumpets, glockenspiel and triangle.

cues.title: The scream of life
cues.text: Around 7:35–7:45 the closing stretch reaches its loudest point on “süßen Duft des Lebens!” — brass with bells up (Schalltrichter auf), cymbal struck with a sponge-headed stick, bass drum. The Mahler Foundation calls this climax the first of the cycle’s whole-tone passages.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows of the closing stretch are 7:35 (−5.1 dB) and 7:40 (−3.1 dB). The score (printed p. 35, rehearsal figure 44) has Schalltr. auf, mit Schwammschlägel and the text; the Mahler Foundation page for this song makes the whole-tone remark, which Wikipedia marks as needing clarification.

cues.title: “Jetzt nehmt den Wein!”
cues.text: The ape’s howl ends and the mood turns: “Jetzt nehmt den Wein! Jetzt ist es Zeit, Genossen! Leert eure goldnen Becher zu Grund!” Now take the wine; empty your golden cups. This is the third refrain’s first half, in A major, with flutes and horns playing slower, held notes.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −3.1 dB at 7:40 to −9.1 dB at 7:45 and −11.1 dB at 7:50 and the key estimate is A major (0.68–0.73) at 7:45–7:50. The score (printed pp. 35–37) has the text, a signature of three sharps, Gehalten and Rit.; Utz Table 2 gives the third refrain as mm. 367–391, with these two verses at mm. 369–379.

cues.title: Emptying the cup, slowly
cues.text: On “zu Grund!” the orchestra nearly stops. Utz measured an extreme ritardando here in this very performance: the refrain’s 35 bars a minute drops to about 12. Listen for how long the singer takes over the last drop before the final “Dunkel ist das Leben”.
cues.evidence: The level falls to −20.6 dB at 8:10 with onset density 1.0 per second and stays low (−13 to −17 dB) at 8:15–8:30. Christian Utz, Musicologica Austriaca (2018), section 3, paragraph 5 and video example 5 (https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37) reports Schuricht’s ritardando at m. 381 from 34.6 to 12.4 bars a minute; the time of m. 381 is proportioned, not measured.

cues.title: Last “Tod”, loud ending
cues.text: The last “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod!” comes a semitone higher still, in A, over harps marked “A dur”. Then a fortissimo Tempo I postlude for the orchestra alone ends the song; the level peaks again near 8:35–8:45 before the sound stops.
cues.evidence: A minor estimated with correlation 0.61–0.80 at 8:10–8:35; level −6.7 and −7.3 dB at 8:35–8:40, then −9.4 dB at 8:45 and −33.3 dB at 8:50. The score (printed pp. 37–38) has Zeit lassen, harps marked “A dur” and Tempo I at figure 48; exact bar times are not claimed.

transitions.title: The loud song sinks into a hush
transitions.how: The opening stanza’s fortissimo drinking music ends and Sempre l’istesso tempo (the same speed) continues in a different world. “Wenn der Kummer naht” is marked düster, zart, and the orchestra thins to quiet strings, harps and a solo violin. The tempo is unchanged on the page, so the effect comes from texture and loudness: the song is still moving, but sorrow now holds the foreground.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 0:58 (0.69) and onset density falling from 3.4 per second at 0:55 to 0.4 at 1:05. The tempo indication, düster zart and thinner scoring are read from printed pp. 8–10 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Ruhig, then sehr ruhig: the refrain
transitions.how: The stanza about the wasted gardens ends on “der Gesang”, and the score slows in two steps: Zurückhaltend. Ruhig., then Sehr ruhig. The tenor’s “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”, sehr getragen, is sung over a solo horn and harp arpeggios in G minor, in a very different register from the loud songs around it. Nothing prepares this moment harmonically; it arrives by slowing.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 1:42 (0.88), low onset density at 1:35–2:00 and G minor estimated at 1:45–2:05. The two tempo markings, solo horn and harp arpeggios are read from printed pp. 11–12 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Tempo I subito returns
transitions.how: The refrain ends on a held “Tod”, and the first speed returns with no preparation: Tempo I subito, with flutter-tongued woodwinds, open trumpets and rushing strings. The stanza about the host’s cellar and the lute is therefore the earlier drinking music in new words. The refrain’s hush is not carried over; each stanza starts again at full force.
transitions.evidence: Level rises from −11.9 dB at 2:00 to −5.1 dB at 2:05 and the loudest windows of the song follow at 2:10–2:20. The tempo marking, tenor’s held Tod and flutter-tonguing are read from printed p. 13 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: The kingdoms of the earth, then sehr ruhig
transitions.how: The wine stanza ends loudly, with “Reiche dieser Erde!”, and the pace slackens again: Rit., then a tempo, sehr ruhig. The second refrain sits a semitone higher than the first, in A♭ rather than G, and again sounds restful beside the music around it. The mutes come off the strings (Dämpfer ab) as the tenor holds the last “Tod”.
transitions.evidence: Level is −7.4 dB at 3:35, then −11.6 dB at 3:40 and −16.5 dB at 3:45, with onset density 0.2 per second at 3:45 and 0.0 at 3:50. The markings and Dämpfer ab are read from printed pp. 21–22 of the 1912 full score; the keys are those of Utz Table 2 (G minor, then A♭).

transitions.title: The voice leaves; the orchestra plays on
transitions.how: After the refrain’s last held “Tod!” the tenor is silent for over a minute. Harps, flutter-tongued flutes, a prominent oboe and marcato trumpet figures carry on in A♭, with Rit. and a tempo markings, and the strings build to sempre ff before the tenor returns at “Das Firmament”. The text pauses; the music uses the time to climb back out of the refrain’s hush.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 3:54 (0.80), then A♭ major estimated at 4:15–5:10 (0.62–0.91) and level −9.4 dB at 4:55–5:00, with a boundary at 5:06 (0.54). The orchestral-only stretch, markings and tenor’s return are read from printed pp. 23–26 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: A diminuendo, then the ape appears
transitions.how: The long reflection on earthly transience ends with “morschen Tande dieser Erde!” and the music dies away: the quietest windows of the song’s second half fall around 6:10–6:15. Then, at rehearsal figure 39, a ff tutti breaks in with glockenspiel, triangle, muted brass and trills, the key signature changes, and the tenor cries “Seht dort hinab!” while strings snap (gerissen). Utz notes the motivic parallel with the song’s opening: the flutter-tongued ritornello returns.
transitions.evidence: The quietest windows are 6:10 and 6:15 (−24.6 and −22.6 dB), then −9.4 dB at 6:20 and the strongest boundary of the song at 6:22 (1.00). The ff tutti, trills, gerissen strings and new signature are read from printed pp. 31–32 of the 1912 full score; the parallel with the opening is Utz’s observation (https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37, section 3).

transitions.title: After the howl, the cups
transitions.how: The howl peaks on “des Lebens!” in brass with bells up, cymbal and bass drum. Then the music relaxes into A major, three sharps, a tempo: the toast “Jetzt nehmt den Wein!” arrives with gentler winds, harps and horn lines, marked Gehalten and Rit. The third refrain begins here, with two verses that the first two refrains do not have. Despair has been staged; the drinkers return to the cups.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −3.1 dB at 7:40 to −9.1 dB at 7:45 and −11.1 dB at 7:50, with A major estimated at 7:45–7:50 (0.68–0.73). Bells-up brass, percussion, the new signature and markings are read from printed pp. 35–36 of the 1912 full score; the two extra verses are noted by Utz (section 3, paragraph 6).

transitions.title: The cup emptied, then a loud Tempo I
transitions.how: “Leert eure goldnen Becher zu Grund!” is followed by a pause in pace: a tempo, Zeit lassen (take your time), and in this performance a very slow ritardando. The tenor then sings the third “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”, in A, with harps marked “A dur”. His last “Tod!” is left open on a diminished chord over the tonic bass, and a loud Tempo I for the orchestra alone ends the song at once.
transitions.evidence: Level is −20.6 dB at 8:10, −13 to −17 dB at 8:15–8:30 and −6.7 and −7.3 dB at 8:35–8:40 before −33.3 dB at 8:50. Zeit lassen, “A dur” on the harps and the final Tempo I are read from printed pp. 37–38 of the 1912 full score; the open diminished-seventh “Tod” and the slow ritardando at m. 381 are described by Utz (section 3, paragraphs 5 and 8).

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, I. Das Trinklied vom Jammer der Erde, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: IMSLP #20582; printed pp. 3–38. Entry times are proportioned between audio anchors at 0:58, 1:42, 2:05, 3:40, 3:54, 6:20, 7:40 and 8:10 and are approximate; which edition the 1939 orchestra used is not documented.

timeline.note: Horns, muted tongued trumpets and trilling woodwinds open the song at full strength.
The tenor enters mit voller Kraft against the full orchestra.
Wenn der Kummer naht: a hushed stanza with harps and a solo violin.
The first refrain: sehr ruhig, a solo horn, harp arpeggios and held strings.
Tempo I subito: flutter-tongued woodwinds, open trumpets and rushing strings.
The tenor addresses the host over trombones, glockenspiel and a full band.
Harp patterns suggest the lute; woodwinds and trombones sustain beneath.
Two solo violins and a solo cello accompany the wine toast, with muted trumpets.
The second refrain, sehr ruhig, a semitone higher; mutes come off the strings.
The orchestra alone: flutter-tongued flutes, a prominent oboe and marcato trumpet figures.
Violins and violas play sempre ff, using the G string, before the voice returns.
The tenor sings Das Firmament blaut ewig over soft winds and strings.
An orchestral subordinate theme in F minor, with the tenor silent.
Du aber, Mensch: the tenor’s question, leidenschaftlich, over a larger band.
Seht dort hinab: trills, brass and snapped strings surround the tenor’s cry.
Muted trumpets, glockenspiel and triangle sound the howl.
The climax: brass with bells up, cymbal and bass drum.
Jetzt nehmt den Wein: a quieter A-major toast with harps and horns.
The slow ritardando on “zu Grund!”, then the third refrain over harps marked A dur.
A fortissimo Tempo I postlude for the orchestra alone ends the song.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
